summary.title: Malleable software: Restoring user agency in a world of locked-down apps
summary.one_liner: Learn why mass-produced software resists personal adaptation and the design patterns (gentle slope, tools not apps, shared data, composable UI) Ink & Switch proposes to make software user-malleable.
takeaways: Settings and plugins only expose what developers anticipated, and plugin systems are siloed per app.
Malleable software aims for minimal-friction adaptation, ideally done in the moment, from small tweaks to deep changes.
A gentle slope lets users move from passive use to creator by avoiding skill cliffs; spreadsheets and HyperCard are examples.
Tools should share data and compose in one workspace rather than living in isolated app silos.
AI code generation alone does not solve malleability; users still need direct, precise control and composable tools.
summary.summary: This Ink & Switch essay argues that personal computing has shifted from malleable physical environments to rigid, mass-produced apps that users cannot easily reshape. It surveys existing customization approaches (settings, plugins, permissionless modding, open source, AI-assisted coding) and explains their limits. It then proposes design patterns for malleable software: a gentle slope of increasing power without skill cliffs, tools instead of single-purpose apps, shared data across tools, and composable user interfaces. The piece is an essay with analogies and references to prior research rather than a how-to.
